content.title: About
content.content: A burrito is a traditional Mexican dish consisting of a large soft wheat tortilla wrapped around a variety of fillings such as meat, beans, rice, cheese, vegetables, and sauces. The NFS (No Fillings Specified) version refers to a basic set of ingredients without additional toppings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Burritos first appeared in the northern regions of Mexico in the early 20th century.
The word “burrito” translates to “little donkey,” though the exact origin of the name is uncertain.
Burritos became popular in the United States in the 1970s thanks to fast‑food chains like Taco Bell.
Traditional Mexican burritos are usually modest in size, while U.S. versions are often oversized.
The NFS option is frequently used in menus to accommodate vegetarians and people with dietary restrictions.

items.title: Balanced macronutrients
items.content: A burrito that includes meat, beans, and rice provides protein, complex carbohydrates, and a modest amount of fat.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Beans and whole‑grain tortillas are rich in dietary fiber, which supports digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and whole grains supply B1, B3, and B6 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Burritos contain iron, magnesium, and zinc, which help maintain immune function and energy production.

items.title: Nutrient density
items.content: When portioned reasonably, a burrito can be a satisfying and nutrient‑dense meal.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Large burritos can be high in calories and fat, which may be undesirable for weight management.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Sauces and processed ingredients often contain a lot of salt, posing a risk for people with hypertension.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Burritos may contain dairy, gluten, and soy, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improperly cooked meat or beans can harbor harmful bacteria or toxins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Burritos are typically served hot. Slice them in half, add fresh veggies, salsa, guacamole, or sour cream. For a lighter option, choose a whole‑grain tortilla and lean meat or plant‑based protein.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared burrito in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For freezing, wrap tightly in plastic film and place in a freezer bag; it keeps up to 2 months. Reheat in the microwave or oven before eating.
